Curriculum

Public Health & Epidemiology

A 119-week curriculum: MPH core, MSc Epidemiology methods, applied biostatistics, and specialist training in pharmacoepidemiology, real-world evidence and the causal evaluation of AI.

12 of 113 lectures written
Block 1 · Foundations, burden of disease and health economics Weeks 1–12 12 of 12 lectures written
  1. 1.1What public health is: core functions, levels of prevention, the three domains
  2. 1.2Rose's prevention paradox: population vs high-risk strategies
  3. 1.3Determinants of health: social, commercial, environmental
  4. 1.4Measuring population health: counts, rates, age standardisation
  5. 1.5Life tables and life expectancy
  6. 1.6Summary measures: YLL, YLD, DALYs, QALYs
  7. 1.7Comparative risk assessment: PAF, PIF, TMREL, and how GBD works
  8. 1.8Nutrition epidemiology: dietary assessment and measurement error
  9. 1.9The salt evidence: salt → blood pressure → cardiovascular disease
  10. 1.10Economic evaluation: costs, perspectives, discounting, ICERs, thresholds
  11. 1.11Decision models: Markov and multistate life tables
  12. 1.12Uncertainty: probabilistic sensitivity analysis and value of information

Project 1: health and economic impact of Saudi salt policies. Model cardiovascular deaths, DALYs and costs averted under the 2019 bread limit and the 2025 voluntary limits (at measured and at full compliance), against WHO benchmarks. Multistate life table model with probabilistic sensitivity analysis and an ML metamodel for value of information.

Block 2 · Epidemiology Weeks 13–32 0 of 20 lectures written
  1. 2.1Measures of frequency and association: risks, rates, odds, ratios, differences
  2. 2.2Cohort studies
  3. 2.3Case-control studies, including nested and case-cohort designs
  4. 2.4Cross-sectional, ecological and case-crossover designs
  5. 2.5Random error: precision, confidence intervals, p-values and their misuse
  6. 2.6Confounding
  7. 2.7Selection bias and collider bias
  8. 2.8Information bias and misclassification
  9. 2.9Effect modification and interaction
  10. 2.10Causation: Bradford Hill and modern causal thinking
  11. 2.11Screening and diagnostic test evaluation
  12. 2.12Systematic reviews and meta-analysis: PICO, search, screening, risk of bias, pooling, PRISMA
  13. 2.13Quantitative bias analysis: how much could bias have changed this result?
  14. 2.14Measurement: validity, reliability and agreement (kappa, ICC, Bland-Altman)
  15. 2.15Clinical epidemiology: diagnostic accuracy and prognosis research
  16. 2.16Pharmacoepidemiology: an introduction (taken to full depth in Block 5)
  17. 2.17Cardiovascular and chronic disease epidemiology: the great cohorts and risk scores
  18. 2.18Life-course and social epidemiology
  19. 2.19Genetic epidemiology and Mendelian randomisation
  20. 2.20Critical appraisal: running a journal club on any epidemiology paper

Project 2: systematic review and meta-analysis of measured salt intake in the GCC. Pool studies that measured salt intake by 24-hour urine in GCC adults, assess their risk of bias, and estimate pooled intake by country and sex.

Block 3 · Biostatistics core Weeks 33–45 0 of 9 lectures written
  1. 3.1Reproducible analysis pipelines for health research
  2. 3.2Statistical computing in R for health data
  3. 3.3GLMs for health data; Poisson and negative binomial models for rates with offsets
  4. 3.4Complex survey design: weights, strata, clusters, design effects
  5. 3.5Missing data and multiple imputation
  6. 3.6Survival analysis: Kaplan-Meier, Cox models, checking proportional hazards
  7. 3.7Competing risks and multistate models
  8. 3.8Longitudinal and clustered data: mixed models vs GEE
  9. 3.9Time series for health data: seasonality, autocorrelation, ARIMA (needed for interrupted time series in Block 4)

Project 3: urinary sodium-to-potassium ratio and cardiovascular mortality (NHANES). A survey-weighted cohort analysis using measured urinary sodium and potassium in NHANES, linked to the public mortality files, with multiple imputation and competing-risks models.

Block 4 · Causal inference and policy evaluation Weeks 46–57 0 of 11 lectures written
  1. 4.1Potential outcomes and identification: exchangeability, positivity, consistency
  2. 4.2DAGs and choosing adjustment sets
  3. 4.3Inverse probability weighting and the g-formula
  4. 4.4Doubly robust estimation, TMLE and machine learning for causal effects
  5. 4.5Target trial emulation
  6. 4.6Difference-in-differences, including staggered adoption and event studies
  7. 4.7Interrupted time series
  8. 4.8Synthetic control
  9. 4.9Regression discontinuity and instrumental variables
  10. 4.10Mediation analysis
  11. 4.11Natural experiments in public health policy

Project 4: did GCC sugary-drink taxes cut consumption? A staggered-adoption difference-in-differences and synthetic control analysis of the GCC excise taxes on sugary drinks. Saudi Arabia and the UAE taxed them in 2017, Bahrain late in 2017, Oman and Qatar in 2019, and Saudi Arabia and the UAE extended the tax to all sweetened drinks in December 2019. Kuwait is the never-taxed comparison; synthetic control adds non-GCC donor countries.

Block 5 · Pharmacoepidemiology, real-world evidence, regulatory science and AI evaluation Weeks 58–74 0 of 17 lectures written
  1. 5.1Pharmacoepidemiology foundations: drug utilisation, defining exposure from prescriptions and dispensing
  2. 5.2New-user and active-comparator designs
  3. 5.3Time-related biases: immortal time, time-window, protopathic bias, reverse causation
  4. 5.4Confounding by indication; propensity scores, including high-dimensional propensity scores
  5. 5.5Self-controlled designs: case-crossover, self-controlled case series
  6. 5.6Real-world data sources: EHRs, claims, registries, linked data; common data models (OMOP)
  7. 5.7Data quality and fitness for purpose; phenotyping and outcome validation
  8. 5.8Statistics of clinical trials: randomisation, intention-to-treat, interim analyses (moved from Block 3)
  9. 5.9Target trial emulation for regulatory decisions; benchmarking against trials
  10. 5.10External and synthetic control arms
  11. 5.11Regulatory science and HTA: how drugs and devices are approved (FDA, EMA, SFDA), how regulators use real-world evidence, and how HTA differs
  12. 5.12Pharmacovigilance: spontaneous reporting, disproportionality analysis, signal detection
  13. 5.13Prediction models in health: development, validation, calibration, TRIPOD+AI (moved from Block 3)
  14. 5.14AI as a medical device: FDA, EU and SFDA regulation; managing model updates
  15. 5.15Causal evaluation of deployed AI: accuracy vs impact; cluster and stepped-wedge trials; difference-in-differences on rollouts
  16. 5.16Post-deployment monitoring: drift, performance decay, feedback loops
  17. 5.17Reporting standards: CONSORT-AI, SPIRIT-AI, DECIDE-AI, RECORD-PE

Project 5A: anticoagulation for new-onset atrial fibrillation in critically ill patients. A target trial emulation in MIMIC-IV, with AF onset defined from the ECG itself (MIMIC-IV-ECG) rather than from diagnosis codes, plus a quantitative bias analysis.

Project 5B: is health AI evaluated for impact, or only for accuracy? A review of the evidence behind FDA-cleared cardiovascular AI devices, including ECG tools: what share were tested prospectively or on patient outcomes, versus retrospective accuracy only.

Block 6 · Health protection Weeks 75–85 0 of 11 lectures written
  1. 6.1Infectious disease epidemiology: transmission, R0, incubation, herd immunity
  2. 6.2Compartmental models: SIR, SEIR, and fitting them to data
  3. 6.3Surveillance systems: notifiable diseases, syndromic and wastewater surveillance
  4. 6.4Outbreak investigation, step by step
  5. 6.5Vaccination programmes: effectiveness, coverage, hesitancy
  6. 6.6Antimicrobial resistance as a public health problem
  7. 6.7Environmental epidemiology: air pollution, exposure assessment
  8. 6.8Spatial epidemiology and small-area estimation (moved from Block 3)
  9. 6.9Heat and health: time series designs and distributed lag non-linear models
  10. 6.10Mass gatherings: the Hajj as a public health case study
  11. 6.11Emergency preparedness and the International Health Regulations

Project 6: heat stress exposure of outdoor workers in the GCC, 1980–2025. Use public climate reanalysis data (ERA5) to compute wet-bulb globe temperature, a measure of heat stress, across GCC cities. Estimate the trend in hours above occupational safety thresholds, and compare it with the region's midday outdoor work bans.

Block 7 · Health improvement and digital health Weeks 86–95 0 of 10 lectures written
  1. 7.1Health promotion: the Ottawa Charter, settings approaches
  2. 7.2Behaviour change theory: COM-B, the Behaviour Change Wheel, Health Belief Model
  3. 7.3Designing interventions: intervention mapping, logic models
  4. 7.4Programme evaluation: process, outcome, realist evaluation
  5. 7.5Health literacy and health communication
  6. 7.6Infodemiology and health misinformation
  7. 7.7Digital health interventions: apps, wearables, chatbots, and their evidence
  8. 7.8Evaluating patient-facing AI: accuracy, safety, bias and readability (builds on Block 5's AI evaluation)
  9. 7.9Mental health in public health
  10. 7.10Tobacco, alcohol and physical activity as public health problems

Project 7: AI chatbot health answers in Gulf Arabic. Test how accurate and safe current AI chatbots are on chronic disease self-management questions (hypertension, diabetes) asked in Gulf dialect vs Modern Standard Arabic, rated by clinicians. Then validate whether an LLM can rate the answers as reliably as clinicians do.

Block 8 · Health systems, policy, global health and equity Weeks 96–107 0 of 12 lectures written
  1. 8.1Health systems: the WHO building blocks, Universal Health Coverage
  2. 8.2Health financing: who pays, how purchasing works
  3. 8.3The Saudi health system: Ministry of Health, SFDA, Saudi Health Council, Vision 2030 Health Sector Transformation
  4. 8.4How policy gets made: Kingdon's streams, evidence-to-policy, policy briefs
  5. 8.5Global health governance: WHO, the IHR, funders, the SDGs
  6. 8.6Social determinants and the Marmot framework
  7. 8.7Measuring health inequality: concentration index, slope and relative index of inequality
  8. 8.8Bayesian hierarchical models and evidence synthesis, for sparse subgroup inputs (moved from Block 3)
  9. 8.9Distributional and extended cost-effectiveness analysis
  10. 8.10Migrant and non-national health in the GCC
  11. 8.11Healthcare public health: service planning, quality, health needs assessment
  12. 8.12Leadership and management in public health organisations

Project 8: who benefits from Saudi salt policy? Extend the Project 1 model with a distributional cost-effectiveness analysis: health gains and costs by sex, region, income and nationality (Saudi nationals vs non-nationals, who differ sharply in age structure and diet).

Block 9 · Research practice, qualitative and mixed methods Weeks 108–119 0 of 11 lectures written
  1. 9.1Writing a study protocol; pre-registration
  2. 9.2Research ethics: consent, secondary data, Saudi review boards (NCBE)
  3. 9.3Qualitative research: paradigms, sampling, rigour
  4. 9.4Document analysis: selecting, sampling and coding policy documents (interviews and focus groups covered briefly)
  5. 9.5Thematic and framework analysis
  6. 9.6Mixed methods designs
  7. 9.7Implementation science: why proven interventions fail in practice (CFIR, RE-AIM)
  8. 9.8Reporting guidelines: STROBE, RECORD, CHEERS, COREQ, PRISMA, TRIPOD+AI
  9. 9.9Peer review and responding to reviewers
  10. 9.10Grant writing and research funding
  11. 9.11Writing a PhD proposal

Project 9: how is Saudi salt policy implemented? A documentary policy analysis of public sources from 2016 to 2026: SFDA standards and technical regulations, the GSO 2612:2025 standard, SFDA reports and announcements, WHO EMRO country reports, industry statements and press coverage. Coded with the CFIR framework, it explains the compliance gap that Project 1 models.
